passage: Layla's phone lit up in the Dublin flat: her classmate Diego's grandmother had died. She didn't know Diego well. She almost typed "She's in a better place," then deleted it, since it sounded like something on a card. She wrote, "Diego, I'm so sorry. I'm here if you want company or help with notes." Two days passed with no reply, and Layla decided not to push. On Friday she left a small tin of tea outside his door with a note: "No need to reply." That evening Diego wrote back a single line of thanks, and later asked if she could sit with him at lunch.

qa.q: What did Layla leave outside Diego's door?
qa.a: Layla left a small tin of tea outside his door.

qa.q: How might Layla have felt writing to Diego, and why did she delete 'She's in a better place'?
qa.a: Layla was probably unsure what to say, since she didn't know Diego well, and deleted the line because it sounded like something on a card, choosing plain, sincere words instead.

qa.q: What could Layla do next to support Diego?
qa.a: Keep in touch lightly, follow up later and offer company or notes without pressure.

qa.q: How might Diego have felt receiving the tea and note?
qa.a: Diego may have felt cared for and relieved that no reply was needed, as his thanks and lunch request suggest.

grounding: A young adult offers condolences with a short sincere message and practical help, and follows up later.

passage: When Afreen heard in the office pantry that her colleague Jagdish's father had died, her first thought was to say something wise. She had nothing. She found Jagdish at his desk, eyes red, and said quietly, "I'm so sorry. I'm here." He nodded. She sat with him for a few minutes without talking. Later she offered to cover his Friday report, and he thanked her with a small, tired smile. A week later, when others had stopped mentioning it, Afreen asked, "How are you doing today?" Jagdish told her that was the first time anyone had asked. She listened for a while and didn't try to fix anything.

qa.q: Where did Afreen hear the news?
qa.a: Afreen heard the news in the office pantry.

qa.q: What did Jagdish's reaction to the question a week later suggest?
qa.a: It suggested Jagdish felt alone in grief once others stopped mentioning it, and was moved that Afreen remembered. The words show a need for follow-up, not only early sympathy.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that helped?
qa.a: She said simple words, sat quietly, offered to cover the report and checked in a week later.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt when colleagues stopped mentioning the loss?
qa.a: Jagdish may have felt overlooked or lonely, since grief lasts longer than the first few days.

grounding: A young adult offers condolences with short words, presence, practical help and follow-up.

passage:
Dear Madhuri,
I heard about your father this morning from Kavya. I'm so sorry. I don't have the right words, and I'm not going to pretend I do.
I only met him once, at your birthday, when he insisted on cutting the cake into perfect squares with a ruler. I've thought about that all day.
You don't need to reply to this. I know your phone must be full.
I'm in Pune till the 20th. If it helps, I can bring food for your family on Thursday, or come and just sit with you. Or I can stay away, if that's easier. Tell me which, or tell me nothing.
I'll call you in a couple of weeks, when everyone else has gone back to normal, just to see how you are.
I'm here.
Hemant

qa.q: When does Hemant offer to bring food?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What does Hemant seem to be feeling as he writes?
qa.a: Hemant seems sad and a little helpless, admitting there are no right words, but caring and eager to be useful.

qa.q: What makes Hemant's condolence helpful rather than clichéd?
qa.a: It is short and sincere, shares one real memory, offers specific practical help, and promises a follow-up call later.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel reading that she doesn't need to reply?
qa.a: Madhuri may feel relieved, since it takes away pressure while the phone is full of messages and grief is heavy.

grounding: Shows a young adult offering condolences with a short sincere message, a specific offer of help and a plan to follow up.

passage: Saurabh, you asked what I say when someone's lost a person. I'm Indu, and I used to get it so wrong. When my friend Reshma's mother died in our second year, I panicked. At the funeral I said, "She's in a better place," and "Everything happens for a reason." Reshma looked at me like I'd slapped her. I went home and cried. So I asked my Nani what to do. She said, "Say less. Be there more." The next week I went to Reshma's house with a box of idlis for the family, and all I said was, "I'm so sorry. I'm here." She hugged me and cried for ten minutes. I didn't say anything else. A month later, when everyone else had stopped calling, I took her for a walk on what would have been her mother's birthday. She still tells me that walk mattered more than all the words at the funeral.

qa.q: What did Indu bring to Reshma's house?
qa.a: A box of idlis for the family.

qa.q: How did Indu feel after the funeral?
qa.a: Indu felt ashamed and upset, going home and crying after seeing how the clichés hurt Reshma.

qa.q: What changed in how Indu offered comfort?
qa.a: Indu said little ("I'm so sorry. I'm here."), brought practical help, and followed up a month later on the birthday.

qa.q: What was it like for Reshma to be remembered a month later?
qa.a: It meant a lot to her, since everyone else had stopped calling and the walk showed Indu still cared.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that simple words, presence, practical help and later follow-up comfort more than clichés.

passage: I'm Himani, and I sat two desks away from Tushar at the bank when our colleague Farooq came back after his brother's death. Most people either avoided Farooq or said long things at the tea counter: "Time heals everything," "Stay strong." I watched Farooq nod at each one, his face blank. Tushar didn't say much at all. On Farooq's first morning back, Tushar put a cup of tea on his desk and said quietly, "I'm really sorry about your brother. If you want me to take the audit calls this week, just say." Farooq nodded. Tushar took the calls. I don't know what Farooq felt, but his shoulders dropped a little. Three weeks later I saw Tushar invite Farooq for lunch, just the two of them. They laughed at something. I'd never seen Farooq laugh since he came back.

qa.q: What did Tushar offer to take for Farooq that week?
qa.a: The audit calls.

qa.q: What might Farooq have been feeling when colleagues said "Time heals everything"?
qa.a: Himani couldn't be sure, but his blank face suggests he felt numb or tired of hearing clichés while grieving.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that others could copy?
qa.a: He said a short sincere sorry, offered specific practical help, and followed up weeks later with lunch.

qa.q: How does Himani see the difference between Tushar and the other colleagues?
qa.a: Himani saw the others either avoid Farooq or offer clichés, while Tushar's few words, practical help and later lunch seemed to ease Farooq.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult offering condolences with simple words, practical help and follow-up instead of clichés.

passage:
Tuesday: When the news came that Urmila's father had died in Jaipur, the class group filled with long messages: "everything happens for a reason", "he's in a better place". Gargi deleted three drafts before sending one line: "Urmila, I'm so sorry. I'm here, whenever." Urmila replied with a single heart.
The following Monday: Urmila was back at the hostel, pale and quiet. Gargi didn't quiz her. She left a steel box of poha outside Urmila's door and a folder of the lab notes she'd missed, with a sticky note: "No need to reply."
Three weeks later: The class had moved on to exam talk. Gargi texted, "Thinking of you today. Want to walk to the tea stall?" Urmila wrote back, "Yes. Everyone else stopped asking." On the walk she talked for twenty minutes about her father's terrible jokes, and laughed once.

qa.q: What did Gargi leave outside Urmila's door?
qa.a: A steel box of poha and a folder of the lab notes she'd missed.

qa.q: Why did Gargi delete three drafts before sending one line?
qa.a: Gargi felt anxious about saying the wrong thing and uneasy with the clichés filling the group, and wanted something short and sincere.

qa.q: What made Gargi's support helpful over time?
qa.a: A simple, sincere message, practical help with no pressure to reply, and a follow-up weeks later when others had stopped asking.

qa.q: What was it like for Urmila three weeks after the loss?
qa.a: She felt others had moved on, since "everyone else stopped asking", so Gargi's invitation let her talk about her father and even laugh.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult offering condolences with a short sincere message, quiet practical help and a later follow-up instead of clichés.
